entry: Atlantic–Congo language of West Africa, spoken mainly in southwestern [[Nigeria]], [[Benin]] and parts of [[Togo]]. It is spoken by the [[Yoruba people]] and has roughly 50 million speakers, including about 2 million second-language speakers. As a pluricentric language, it forms a dialect continuum with smaller communities in Côte d'Ivoire, Sierra Leone and Gambia. Yoruba-derived vocabulary serves as a liturgical language in Afro-Brazilian and Caribbean religions such as Candomblé and Santería. It is the principal Yoruboid language, most closely related to Itsekiri and Igala. The earliest known grammar and dictionary appeared in 1849, produced by Yoruba communities in Sierra Leone. Its Latin-alphabet orthography was developed by missionaries in the 19th century and refined by a 1966 committee.

West African ethnic group inhabiting Yorubaland in parts of [[Nigeria]], [[Benin]] and [[Togo]]. The Yoruba number more than 50 million in Africa and over a million elsewhere, most of them in Nigeria, where they make up 20.7 percent of the population according to Ethnologue estimates. Most speak the [[Yoruba language]]. The Yoruba emerged largely in situ from earlier Volta-Niger populations by the 1st millennium BCE, and by the 5th century BCE a powerful city-state existed at Ile-Ife. The Ife Empire, the first empire in Yoruba history, flourished between 1200 and 1420 CE across much of southwestern Nigeria, eastern Benin and Togo. Later, the [[Oyo Empire]] dominated regional trade and military affairs from the 17th to early 19th centuries. Yoruba communities are also represented in the African diaspora in [[Brazil]], [[Cuba]] and the Caribbean.

Traditional religious and spiritual system of the [[Yoruba people]], also called Orisha or Isese. Its homeland is Yorubaland in southwestern [[Nigeria]], southern [[Benin]] and central [[Togo]]. It is considered the largest indigenous African religion, with several million adherents worldwide. It is a form of diffused monotheism, with a supreme but distant creator force served by intermediary orishas and by ancestors. The Yoruba believe in the possibility of [[Reincarnation|reincarnation]] within the family. Central practice is Ifá [[Divination|divination]], which consults verses through binary patterns inscribed on boards or palm nuts. The religion shares parallels with Vodun and is the basis for several religions in the New World, notably Santería in [[Cuba]] and Candomblé in [[Brazil]].

National park in the [[Sierra Nevada]] of [[California]], United States. Designated a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1984 for its [[Granite|granite]] cliffs, waterfalls, giant sequoia groves and biological diversity, it is almost 95 percent designated wilderness. It is one of the largest and least fragmented habitat blocks in the range. The Sierra Nevada was uplifted about 10 million years ago, and later glaciers carved the U-shaped Yosemite Valley. Native Americans inhabited the region for nearly 4,000 years before European Americans arrived by 1833. The Yosemite Grant of 1864, signed by [[Abraham Lincoln]], declared Yosemite federally preserved land. In 1890 [[John Muir]] led a successful movement to establish Yosemite Valley and its surrounding areas as a national park. It draws about four million visitors annually.

American online video-sharing platform owned by [[Google]]. Founded on February 14, 2005, by Chad Hurley, Jawed Karim and Steve Chen, former employees of [[PayPal]], it is headquartered in San Bruno, California. It is the second-most-visited website in the world, after Google itself, with more than 2.7 billion monthly active users in January 2024. Google purchased YouTube on November 13, 2006, for 1.65 billion USD and expanded its business model beyond [[Advertising|advertising]] to paid offerings such as YouTube Premium. Video categories range from [[Music video|music videos]] and [[News|news]] to films, vlogs and live streams, and most submissions come from individuals. Critics argue that the platform has facilitated misinformation and copyrighted material, violated users' privacy, engaged in excessive censorship, and enforced its guidelines inconsistently.

Phase of the human life span at the onset of adulthood, following [[Adolescence|adolescence]]. Definitions vary. The United States Census Bureau defines young adults as people aged 18 to 34, while cancer researchers use 18 to 49. [[Erik Erikson]]'s stages of human development significantly shaped the concept, describing this stage as focused on [[Intimate relationship|intimate relationships]] and personal identity. It precedes [[Middle age|middle adulthood]], which is often associated with stability in career and relationships. Some developmental researchers call it "emerging adulthood," a period of continued brain maturation into the early 30s. Young adults tend to have lower voter turnout than people of middle or older age. The phrase is also used to market young adult novels aimed at readers as young as 13 or 14, a broader use that has been disputed.

Mechanical property of solid materials measuring tensile or compressive stiffness. It is the ratio of stress (force per unit area) to axial strain in the linear elastic region of a material, similar to the spring constant in [[Hooke's law]] but with dimensions of pressure. It is named after the 19th-century British scientist [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]], although the concept was developed in 1727 by [[Leonhard Euler]]. Values are usually given in gigapascals (GPa); aluminum has a high value and rubber a low one. The term derives from the Latin modus, meaning measure.

International multi-sport event for athletes aged 15 to 18, organized by the International Olympic Committee (IOC). It is held every four years in summer and winter editions, with the winter Games in leap years. The first summer edition took place in [[Singapore]] in 2010 and the first winter edition in [[Austria]] in 2012. The IOC approved the event in 2007. The next summer Games are scheduled for [[Dakar]] in 2026, and the next winter Games for 2028 in the [[Dolomites]] and Valtellina, Italy. In 2026, IOC president Kirsty Coventry announced a pause on awarding future editions.

Metallic [[Chemical element|chemical element]] (symbol Yb, atomic number 70) of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series. Swiss chemist Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated it in 1878 from the rare earth erbia and named it for Ytterby, the Swedish village near where the component was found. Pure metal was first obtained in 1953. Natural ytterbium is a mixture of seven stable isotopes, present at an average of 3 parts per million in the Earth's crust. It is mined mainly in China, the United States, [[Brazil]] and India, chiefly as the mineral monazite. Ytterbium is used mainly as a dopant in [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]] and in laser media, and less often as a gamma-ray source. Prepared ytterbium is somewhat hazardous as an eye and skin irritant, and the metal is a fire and explosion hazard.

Silvery [[Transition metal|transition metal]] (symbol Y, atomic number 39) chemically similar to the [[Lanthanide|lanthanides]]. It is almost always found with lanthanide elements in rare-earth [[Mineral|minerals]] and never occurs free in nature. Its only stable isotope, ⁸⁹Y, is the only one found in the Earth's crust. It was named after the mineral ytterbite, first identified in 1787 in the Swedish village of Ytterby. Its most important present use is in phosphors, especially for LEDs; it was once widely used in red phosphors in [[Cathode ray tube|cathode ray tubes]] of television sets. It also goes into electrodes, electrolytes, electronic filters, [[Laser|lasers]], superconductors and medical applications. Yttrium has no known biological role, but exposure to its compounds can cause lung disease.

Legendary sage-king of ancient China and founder of the [[Xia dynasty]]. He is credited with the first successful state efforts at flood control and is praised for his upright character by [[Confucius]] and other Chinese teachers. He is one of the few Chinese monarchs posthumously honored with the epithet "the Great." There is no contemporary evidence of his existence. He is said to have ruled in the late 3rd millennium BC, but his name does not appear on artifacts from that era or on the later [[Shang dynasty]] oracle bones; it first appears on vessels from the Western Zhou period (c. 1045–771 BC). According to [[Sima Qian]]'s Shiji (c. 90 BC), his father was Gun, and his great-great-grandfather was the [[Yellow Emperor]].

Mongol-led imperial dynasty of China (1271–1368), founded by [[Kublai Khan]]. Its official name was Great Yuan, and it succeeded the [[Song dynasty]] and preceded the [[Ming dynasty]]. It was a successor state to the [[Mongol Empire]]. Kublai proclaimed the dynasty in 1271 in the traditional Han style, and the conquest was completed in 1279 with the defeat of the Southern Song at the Battle of Yamen. It was the first dynasty founded by a non-Han ethnicity to rule all of China proper. Kublai relocated the capital to Dadu, modern [[Beijing]], and the dynasty repaired the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]] and fostered Eurasian trade that spread porcelain westward. After the Ming defeated the Yuan forces in 1368, the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau, where they ruled as the Northern Yuan until 1635.

Large, low-relief [[Peninsula|peninsula]] of southeastern [[Mexico]] and adjoining parts of Belize and Guatemala. It separates the [[Gulf of Mexico]] from the [[Caribbean Sea]] and is almost entirely made of porous [[Limestone|limestone]], with karst features such as cenotes, or sinkholes. The [[Chicxulub crater]] was formed about 66 million years ago by an asteroid roughly 10 to 15 kilometers across, at the end of the [[Cretaceous]] period. Human occupation is ancient: in 2020, divers excavated Chan Hol cave near Tulum and found the skeleton of a woman who lived at least 9,900 years ago. The peninsula was the heartland of the pre-Columbian Maya civilization, which flourished from around 2000 BCE until the Spanish conquest, and it is home to sites such as Chichén Itzá and Uxmal.

Plant genus of the agave subfamily, native to North America from Panama to southern Canada, with 50 accepted species. Species range from small shrubs to tree-like forms such as the Joshua tree, which can reach 15 meters (49 feet). Yuccas are xerophytes with rosettes of pointed leaves and large, cream-white flowers. Their relationship with the yucca moths that pollinate them is a well-known example of evolutionary [[Pollination|mutualism]]. The plants provide shelter in North American deserts, and some species grow in the [[Rocky Mountains]] and [[Great Plains]]. Flower petals are eaten in local cuisine in Central America and Mexico, and fibers were historically woven into cords, baskets, mats and sandals. Native peoples still use the plant to make traditional soaps.

Branch of the [[Chinese language|Sinitic languages]] spoken mainly in the provinces of [[Guangdong]] and Guangxi in southern China. Linguists reserve the name [[Cantonese]] for the prestige variety of [[Guangzhou]], [[Hong Kong]] and [[Macau]], although the term is often used for the whole branch. Yue languages are not mutually intelligible with each other or with other Chinese languages outside the branch. They are among the most conservative varieties in final consonants and tonal categories of Middle Chinese, though they have lost several distinctions in initial consonants. Large-scale Han Chinese migration into the Lingnan area began after the Qin conquest in 214 BC; later migrants included Hakka and Min speakers. The branch has about 85 million native speakers, second only to Mandarin.

Series of ethnic conflicts and wars of independence in the former [[Yugoslavia]] from 1991 to 2001. They both led to and resulted from the breakup of Yugoslavia into six states. Many war crimes were committed, including [[Genocide|genocide]], ethnic cleansing and mass wartime rape. The [[United Nations]] established the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in [[The Hague]] to prosecute them. Often described as one of Europe's deadliest conflicts since [[World War II]], they caused an estimated 140,000 deaths according to the International Center for Transitional Justice and at least 130,000 casualties according to the Humanitarian Law Center.

Country in [[Central Europe]] and the [[Balkans]] that existed from 1918 to 1992; its name means "Land of the South Slavs." Formed after [[World War I]] as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, it was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929. [[Axis powers|Axis]] forces invaded in April 1941. Communist-led Partisans under [[Josip Broz Tito]] ruled from 1944 until Tito's death, and in 1963 the country became the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, with six republics: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia and Slovenia. After economic crisis and rising nationalism, it broke up along its republics' borders during the [[Revolutions of 1989]], leading to the [[Yugoslav Wars]]. The reduced federation of Serbia and Montenegro was dissolved in 2006.

Japanese writer and nationalist activist, born Kimitake Hiraoka. He is considered one of the most important postwar stylists of the Japanese language. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in the 1960s, and the award went in 1968 to his countryman and benefactor [[Yasunari Kawabata]]. His works include the novels *Confessions of a Mask* and *The Temple of the Golden Pavilion*. From his mid-30s his nationalist and reactionary views became increasingly evident; he opposed Western-style materialism, postwar democracy and [[Communism|communism]]. In 1968 he formed the Tatenokai, a private militia to protect the dignity of the emperor. He and four of its members seized the commandant of a military base in central [[Tokyo]] and urged the Self-Defense Forces to rise against Article 9 of the 1947 Constitution. The attempt failed, and he died by seppuku, which he had planned.

Westernmost and smallest territory of [[Canada]] by land area (pop., 2026: 50,356). It borders [[British Columbia]], the [[Northwest Territories]], the [[Beaufort Sea]] and the U.S. state of [[Alaska]]. Its capital, [[Whitehorse]], is the largest city in northern Canada. A federal [[Statute|statute]] split it from the Northwest Territories in 1898. Mount Logan, at 5,959 meters (19,551 feet), is Canada's highest mountain. Most of the territory has a subarctic climate. The name derives from the [[Yukon River]].

Major watercourse of northwestern North America, flowing from [[British Columbia]] through [[Yukon]] to the [[Bering Sea]]. The lower half flows through [[Alaska]], and at 3,190 km (1,980 mi) it is the longest river in both Alaska and Yukon. It empties into the Bering Sea at the Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta. Its total drainage area is 854,700 sq km (330,000 sq mi), of which 323,800 sq km lies in Canada. Paddle-wheel [[Riverboat|riverboats]] carried traffic during the Klondike Gold Rush and plied the river until the 1950s. The river has a history of pollution from military installations and dumps, though the Environmental Protection Agency does not list it among impaired watersheds. A council of 70 First Nations and tribes works toward making the river safe to drink from again.

Russian-born American actor, known for playing King Mongkut in *The King and I*. Born in Vladivostok into a Swiss-Russian family, he won two Tony Awards for the [[Rodgers and Hammerstein]] musical and an Academy Award for Best Actor for the 1956 film adaptation. He became known for his shaved head, which he kept as a trademark. His films include *The Ten Commandments* and *The Magnificent Seven*. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960. He died of [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]].

Inland province of southwestern China, bordering [[Myanmar]], [[Vietnam]] and [[Laos]] (pop., 2020: 47,209,277). Its capital is [[Kunming]]. The province spans about 394,000 sq km, with high mountains in the northwest and most of its population in the east. It has the largest diversity of plant life in China, with perhaps 17,000 of the country's roughly 30,000 vascular plant species. Its reserves of aluminum, lead, zinc and tin are the largest in China, and it has major copper and nickel reserves. Parts of the province formed the Dian Kingdom in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC, until the [[Han dynasty]] conquered it in the late 2nd century BC. Ethnic minorities make up about 34 percent of the population, including Yi, Bai, Hani, Zhuang, Dai and Miao. Yunnan is identified as the birthplace of [[Tea|tea]] and as the region of origin of the plant genus [[Cannabis]].

Highland region of southwest [[China]], spread mainly over [[Yunnan]] and Guizhou provinces. Under its strictest definition it stretches from the Red River Fault in Yunnan to the Wuling Mountains in Hunan, covering most of eastern Yunnan and Guizhou. Its southwest is a true plateau with flatter highlands, while the northeast is mountainous, with rolling hills, gorges and karst topography. The plateau separates the Sichuan Basin from South China and has long been considered a backwater; it is among China's most economically depressed regions. Major cities include [[Kunming]], Guiyang and Zunyi. The world's highest bridge, the Beipanjiang Bridge, spans the Yunnan–Guizhou border. The western plateau drains mainly through the Nanpan and Beipan rivers, headwaters of the [[Pearl River]], while the eastern part is largely drained by the Wu River, a tributary of the [[Yangtze]].

Soviet politician, general secretary of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] from late 1982. He chaired the [[KGB]] from 1967 to 1982 and was earlier ambassador to Hungary, where he took part in suppressing the 1956 uprising. He succeeded [[Leonid Brezhnev]] in November 1982 and pursued drives against corruption, absenteeism and economic inefficiency. Under his leadership the [[Cold War]] intensified and the regime struggled with the economic crisis. He promoted a generation of reformers, most importantly [[Mikhail Gorbachev]]. He led the [[Soviet Union]] for only about 15 months.

Soviet pilot and cosmonaut, the first person to journey into [[Outer space|outer space]]. He was launched from Baikonur in the Kazakh SSR aboard [[Vostok 1]] and completed one orbit of Earth on 12 April 1961 in a flight of 108 minutes. The flight was a milestone for the [[Soviet Union]] in the [[Space Race]], and it made him an international celebrity and Hero of the Soviet Union. Born to a farming family in the Russian SFSR, he trained as a foundryman and joined the Soviet Air Forces as a pilot. His village was occupied during [[World War II]]. Officials barred him from further spaceflights after the fatal crash of Soyuz 1, which killed his friend Vladimir Komarov, and he later became deputy training director of the Cosmonaut Training Centre. He died when the MiG-15 he was piloting crashed near Kirzhach.
